solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Also do without lines about beginning to manage a firm

blocks.note: to forgo something is to do without it
a poem is lines of verse
A plus SURE, firm as in steady or certain

explanation.surface: A boss is told to cut staff lines while taking over the running of a company.
explanation.walkthrough: FORGO + OD(M)E + A SURE. 'Also' looks too slight to be a definition, but 'for good measure' is exactly an 'as well' tacked on.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means as an extra addition on top of what was given, so it works as a synonym in sentences.

clue.text: Excited, ditching last of pear, swallowing a nut

blocks.note: excited to the point of frenzy
the article kept as it stands

explanation.surface: Someone is thrilled about a fruit and nut snack, dropping the pear and gulping down a nut.
explanation.walkthrough: FRANTIC loses R to give FANTIC, which then swallows A. The surface makes 'nut' food, but it is the definition, the enthusiast sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A nut is informal for an obsessive enthusiast or devotee, as in a fitness nut, which is a zealot.

clue.text: Determine hidden structures in greeneries never uprooted

indicators.note: plants pulled up are left in disorder, so the letters of the plant words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A gardener works out what lies beneath plants that have never been dug up.
explanation.walkthrough: The gardening surface hides a technical definition: taking apart a finished product to discover how it was designed and built.
explanation.definitionFit: To reverse-engineer a product is to analyse it backwards to work out its inner design and workings.

clue.text: Just working lazily, not putting heart into it

blocks.note: a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: Someone is barely working, half-heartedly going through the motions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not putting heart into it' reads as a description of idleness but instructs you to drop the middle of 'lazily'.
explanation.definitionFit: Just and this word are adverb synonyms meaning merely or no more than, as in just a child.

clue.text: Fell wood, involving daughter before end of day

blocks.note: deal is pine or fir timber

explanation.surface: A father chops down trees with his daughter helping before the day is out.
explanation.walkthrough: DEA(D)L + Y. 'Fell' looks like the verb for cutting timber, but it is the old adjective meaning cruel or lethal, as in 'one fell swoop'.
explanation.definitionFit: Fell as an adjective is an archaic word for fierce, savage or lethal, so it matches this synonym.

clue.text: Spiritual, with other writers coming round at this point

blocks.note: et al., 'and others', used when citing several authors
here means at this place or moment

explanation.surface: A mystical author finds fellow writers visiting at this very moment.
explanation.walkthrough: ET AL is the Latin abbreviation used in reference lists for 'and others', typically co-authors, so 'other writers' is a fair hint.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something unworldly and heavenly rather than physical, making them adjective synonyms.

clue.text: Expert turned up old records on American espionage targets?

blocks.note: EPs, extended-play records of the vinyl era
the question mark marks a CIA list as the agency's roster of targets

explanation.surface: An expert has dug out old files on American spying targets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Records' is the vinyl kind, not files. The question mark flags that 'American espionage targets' is read whimsically as a CIA list.
explanation.definitionFit: An expert is someone with deep knowledge of one particular field, which is what this noun names.

clue.text: House unfinished? Adult suppressing anger to get acceptable warmth

blocks.note: to room is to house or lodge someone; drop the final letter
a flash of temper is anger

explanation.surface: In a half-built house a grown-up keeps their temper in check while trying to get comfortably warm.
explanation.walkthrough: ROO(M) + M(TEMPER)ATURE. 'House' is the verb, as in to room with someone, which shares its first four letters with the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the comfortable ordinary indoor heat level at which wine is served, a normal ambient level.

clue.text: Studies climbing and thanks uphill Alpine vehicle

blocks.note: to con is to study or learn

explanation.surface: Mountaineers climbing a slope thank the driver of a vehicle going uphill in the Alps.
explanation.walkthrough: To con is an old verb for studying closely; TA is British slang for thanks. A Sno-Cat is a tracked vehicle for travel over snow.
explanation.definitionFit: A tracked snow tractor used on mountains and ski slopes, of which the Alps provide a typical setting.

clue.text: American railway line seen in star’s short book

blocks.note: the el, an elevated railway in US cities
a star that suddenly flares in brightness

explanation.surface: A celebrity's slim volume features a US railway line.
explanation.walkthrough: The EL is Chicago-style shorthand for an elevated railway. The ''s' on 'star' is just 'has', joining star to the book.
explanation.definitionFit: A novella is a work of fiction longer than a story yet shorter than a full novel.

clue.text: American dance aspired to ditch piano – now under review

indicators.note: something under review is being reworked

explanation.surface: A dancer who hoped to drop the piano accompaniment now has the routine being reassessed.
explanation.walkthrough: HOPED minus P, then NOW mixed up. The surface reads 'American dance' as the subject of the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoedown is a lively rural US folk gathering with square dancing and fiddle music.

clue.text: Satisfied about Republican going over time in office

indicators.note: going over is turning over, so the whole combination flips

blocks.note: met, as a demand or need is met

explanation.surface: A contented Republican politician is serving beyond the limit of an elected stint.
explanation.walkthrough: M(R)ET read backwards. 'Going over time' tempts as a phrase about overrunning, but 'going over' is the reversal and 'time in office' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A term is the fixed period during which an official holds a post, such as a presidency.

clue.text: Victorian heroine mostly inspiring confidence about one putting others first

blocks.note: Lewis Carroll's heroine, less her last letter

explanation.surface: A heroine of a Victorian novel nearly always gives others confidence through her selfless nature.
explanation.walkthrough: The Victorian heroine is Lewis Carroll's Alice. 'One putting others first' looks like the definition, but the answer is an adjective, so 'one' belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Being selfless and caring for other people before oneself is the meaning of this adjective.

clue.text: English city style identifying English author

blocks.note: surface padding that narrows the city to one in England; it gives no letters
ton, as in fashionable style or high society

explanation.surface: A city's particular style makes it clear which writer is being described.
explanation.walkthrough: TON for style is dated, from the French 'bon ton'. G.K. Chesterton wrote the Father Brown detective stories.
explanation.definitionFit: G. K. Chesterton was an English writer, critic and creator of the Father Brown detective tales.

clue.text: Nursery‘s curtailed set of principles restraining children

indicators.note: curtailed means its tail is cut

blocks.note: a creed, without its last letter

explanation.surface: A nursery has cut back its rulebook for keeping children under control.
explanation.walkthrough: CRE(CH)E, from CREE(D). A crèche is a day nursery for young children, the French word being usual in British English.
explanation.definitionFit: A creche is a place where babies and toddlers are looked after, the same as a day nursery.

clue.text: Cheers complaint about male addition to board?

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles about a man being appointed to a company board.
explanation.walkthrough: TA + BLE(M)AT. 'Board' is the dining table in the old sense, with the question mark flagging the stretch; the surface wants a boardroom.
explanation.definitionFit: A mat placed under plates is literally an extra item added to the dining table, the old sense of board.

clue.text: Philosopher‘s tense abandoning collection for union?

blocks.note: a bride's collection of clothes and linen gathered for her marriage

explanation.surface: A thinker is nervous about leaving a trade union.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove T from TROUSSEAU. 'Tense' looks like an adjective about the philosopher's mood; 'union' is marriage, not a trade union.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was an eighteenth-century Genevan thinker who wrote The Social Contract.

clue.text: Beach and garden footwear?

blocks.note: to hoe is to garden, weeding the soil

explanation.surface: Someone asks what shoes to wear on the beach and in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Garden' is a verb here. A sandshoe is the British name for a plimsoll, a light canvas shoe with rubber sole, worn on the beach.
explanation.definitionFit: A sandshoe is a canvas plimsoll with a rubber sole, a type of casual shoe worn on beaches.

clue.text: Blue Tory gutted to support upwardly mobile corporations

indicators.note: a gutted fish has its insides removed
in a down clue, a piece that supports another sits beneath it

blocks.note: a corporation is jocularly a pot belly, so tums

explanation.surface: A Conservative, sad and gutted, props up ambitious big businesses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue' looks like the Tory colour or sadness but means rude. 'Corporations' is old slang for paunches, which is why tums fit.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue can describe jokes or films that are indecent or obscene, a sense shared with this adjective.

clue.text: Out for the count, when sheltered and quiet

blocks.note: as meaning at the time that
the lee is the sheltered side

explanation.surface: A knocked-out boxer is lying somewhere calm and protected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out for the count' sounds like boxing, but the idiom also describes someone fast in slumber.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone deeply unconscious or sleeping soundly, not just knocked out in a ring.

clue.text: Pastoral god yonder, hiding tail, in form of cat

blocks.note: Pan, Greek god of shepherds and flocks

explanation.surface: A rustic god over there, tail tucked away, has taken the shape of a cat.
explanation.walkthrough: PAN + THER(E). The shape-shifting god fits Greek myth, where gods often took animal form.
explanation.definitionFit: A panther is a large wild feline, usually a black leopard, so it is one kind of big cat.

clue.text: Brood about overturned craft in water channel

blocks.note: a hen broods, or sits, on her eggs
a craft is a skill or art

explanation.surface: Someone sulks over a capsized boat in a waterway.
explanation.walkthrough: S(TRA)IT. 'Craft' reads as a boat in this watery surface, but it is skill.
explanation.definitionFit: A strait is a narrow passage of sea linking two larger bodies of water, like the Dover one.

clue.text: French article, one with truth about opening for students in the Sorbonne?

explanation.surface: A French paper reports on a place opening for students at the Sorbonne.
explanation.walkthrough: UN + I + VER(S)ITY. The question mark marks the definition as an example: the Sorbonne is one instance of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sorbonne in Paris is a famous example of a higher education institution granting degrees.

clue.text: Time off school? Wet weather

blocks.note: to school someone is to train them

explanation.surface: A child asks whether bad weather means a day off school.
explanation.walkthrough: TRAIN minus T. 'Time off school' looks like a holiday, but 'school' is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Water falling from clouds in drops is the most common damp form of precipitation.

clue.text: Regularly meet Italian poet, withholding name

blocks.note: Dante Alighieri, author of the Divine Comedy

explanation.surface: An Italian poet is seen often but keeps his name secret.
explanation.walkthrough: DANTE minus N. 'Regularly' looks like an alternate-letters instruction, but it belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To date someone is to go out with them routinely in a romantic relationship.

clue.text: Articles about limiting temperature in part of hospital

explanation.surface: Hospital notices talk about controlling the temperature on a ward.
explanation.walkthrough: THE A + T + RE. In British English an operating theatre is where surgery takes place.
explanation.definitionFit: The operating theatre is the surgical room within a hospital, so it is one section of it.

clue.text: Pub in Australia opening for Halloween if necessary

blocks.note: a tap or taproom is a bar

explanation.surface: An Australian bar will open for Halloween if there is demand.
explanation.walkthrough: A(TAP)US + H. The British idiom means with some effort or if really needed.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means only with difficulty or when absolutely required, matching the conditional phrase.

clue.text: Follow everything to raise that girl in hurry

blocks.note: to bring up children is to raise them
to tear along is to rush

explanation.surface: Someone does all they can to bring up a daughter while rushing about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Follow' alone looks like the definition, but 'everything' is needed: the phrase means come behind all the others. 'To tear' is British for dashing.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to be last in a line or procession, coming behind all the others.
